               REPLIES TO EXCEPTIONS TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

           Whitis Land Investments, LP (Whitis) files these Replies to Exceptions to the Proposal for

Decision (“PFD”). The Exceptions should be overruled. The PFD correctly recognizes that the

Commission’s approval of a regional plan authorized the filing of certificate applications; it did

not relieve the Joint Applicants of their burden to prove in this contested case that Import Path 2

is necessary under PURA § 37.056. The PFD also correctly enforces the Commission’s notice

rules against the filed project—not merely the smaller preliminary network shown nine months

earlier.

                                 I.     REPLIES TO JOINT APPLICANTS

A. Applicants’ Exception B.1 Does Not Displace the PFD’s Project-Specific Findings on the
   Forecasted Loads

           Applicants except to Finding of Fact Nos. 87–111 and Conclusion of Law Nos. 13 and 14,

arguing that changed circumstances affirm—rather than undermine—the need for Import Path 2. 1

The exception is incorrect because an unstudied change in circumstances does less to establish

need than the Application’s unreliable data. Instead, Applicants continue to rest on approval of the


1
    Applicants’ Exceptions at 13–20.

Intervenor: Whitis Land Investments, LP
Reply To Exceptions to Proposal for Decision                                             Page 1 of 10
 PBRP, continued inclusion of the three import paths in later planning models, and an unquantified

aggregate regional load growth. The Commission’s October 2024 PBRP Order authorized the

applicable TSPs to prepare CCN applications, but required each TSP to establish that the CCN

meets “all applicable legal requirements,” including the need requirement from PURA § 37.056. 2

In April 2025, the Commission selected the 765-kV voltage option without eliminating that

project-specific requirement. 3

        Applicants conflate the PFD’s findings that applying ERCOT’s adjusted load forecasting

would result in a material reduction with a “non-expert reduction” in the Permian Basin load

forecasts. The record supports the need for a reexamination of ERCOT’s load forecasting

methodology. ERCOT acknowledged that need, and the Commission agreed. In 2025, ERCOT

adopted, and the Commission approved, an adjusted load-forecasting methodology because

forecasted loads had entered service at lower levels than anticipated. Applicants did not provide

an analysis retesting the PBRP forecast under that methodology or otherwise verify that the

underlying contracts, officer-letter loads, and unconfirmed loads remained on the forecast

trajectory. Applicants offered only that the stack of requests continued to grow “directionally.” 4

Staff witness John Poole agreed that changed conditions warranted reevaluation. 5

        Applicants’ evidence of growth in the Permian Basin and later planning activity does not

answer that defect. Aggregate regional growth does not:

             a. identify which forecasted loads require Import Path 2,

             b. establish that those loads will materialize, or

             c. quantify the line’s independent necessity.

 Likewise, HB 5066 required the Commission to consider historical load, forecasted growth, and

exempt Applicants from proving need under PURA § 37.056(a). The PFD did not recommend the

retroactive amendment of the PBRP; it evaluated the present CCN record and found that the

forecasted loads, in light of changed circumstances, did not establish need for these Projects.

           Whitis respectfully requests that the Commission overrule Applicants’ Exception B.1 and

retain Finding of Fact Nos. 87–111 and Conclusion of Law Nos. 13 and 14.

B. Applicants’ Exception B.2: Evidence Regarding Far West Texas Import GTCs Does
   Not Establish Import Path 2’s Independent Need

           Applicants except to Finding of Fact Nos. 112–116 and argue that the Far West Texas

Import GTCs provide a separate, present-day reliability basis that independently requires approval

of Import Path 2 by 2030. The exception asks the Commission to make the analytical jump from

evidence of regional operating constraints to the unsupported conclusion that Import Path 2 is

independently necessary to resolve them.

           The record reflects that ERCOT’s April 2026 presentation identifies the three import paths

collectively as one of seven upgrades expected to “help” exit the GTCs; it does not identify Import

Path 2 as the sole solution or quantify its independent effect. 6 Mr. Martin testified that the GTCs

had not resulted in load shed and that price-responsive cryptocurrency mining and battery behavior

had provided operating margin. 7 However, Applicants failed to show:

               a. whether the GTCs could be retired without Import Path 2,

               b. which of the listed upgrades supplies what relief, or

               c. what portion of the constrained load is durable.




6
    App. Ex. 14 (Martin Reb.), CMM-R-5 at Bates 42.
7
    App. Ex. 14 (Martin Reb.) at 9, 15; PFD at 83.

Intervenor: Whitis Land Investments, LP
Reply To Exceptions to Proposal for Decision                                             Page 3 of 10
 The evidence supports the PFD’s distinction between proof of a regional constraint and proof that

Import Path 2 is a necessary remedy.

         Whitis respectfully requests that the Commission overrule Applicants’ Exception B.2 and

retain Finding of Fact Nos. 112–116.

C. Applicants’ Exception B.3: Applicants Fail to Provide Proof That the Line Can
   Perform Its Asserted Import Function

         Applicants except to Finding of Fact Nos. 117–127, arguing that the PFD improperly

required identification of particular generators at Bell County East and misunderstood an

interconnected, bidirectional transmission system. The exception fails because the PFD did not

require Import Path 2 to operate as a generator-specific tie. The PFD required evidence that

sufficient power would be available on the eastern end of Import Path 2 to perform the westbound

import function used to justify them.

         Applicants rely on the 2025 RTP to support the need for Import Path 2 to transport power

from other regions into the Permian Basin due to offset large loads and insufficient local

conventional generation. Yet, the 2025 RTP states that Central Texas itself needs additional import

capability. 8 Ms. Cooley testified that no additional generation would be added at Bell County East.
9
    Applicants never identified where the power needed to supply the westbound transfer would

come. They also failed to demonstrate Central Texas’s net generation position. Applicants

certainly could not prove that Central Texas has a surplus load available for export. 10 Mr. Martin

and Mr. Gurley could only provide generalized statements that Bell County East was a “strong

system node” that establishes connectivity, not available energy. 11 Physical bidirectionality shows

only what the line can do if power is available. It does not prove the availability of the power

necessary for the studied import function.


8
  App. Ex. 17 (Gurley Reb.), JG-R-3 at 30–32; PFD at 85–86.
9
  Tr. Vol. 3 at 120:14–16.
10

          Whitis respectfully requests that the Commission overrule Applicants’ Exception B.3 and

retain Finding of Fact Nos. 117–127.

D. Applicants’ Exception B.4: The PBRP Does Not Establish Import Path 2’s Independent
   Need by 2030

         Applicants except to Finding of Fact Nos. 128–131 and argue that the PFD invented a

partial-build-study requirement because the PBRP studied the three import paths as an integrated

system. The exception misstates the PFD. The PFD prescribed no particular study format; it found

that Applicants offered no evidence separating Import Path 2 from the three-path package and thus

did not prove that this particular path is independently needed by 2030.

         PURA § 37.056 requires Applicants to prove the need for the facilities proposed in this

CCN application. 12 The Commission’s PBRP Order likewise required each responsible TSP to

establish all applicable legal requirements in the later CCN proceeding. 13 Regional NERC

contingencies may explain why ERCOT studied multiple paths, but they do not establish which

individual path must be built by 2030. 14

         The record reflects that Mr. Gurley knew of no study isolating Import Path 2 or testing a

partial build. His explanation that N-1 and N-1-1 criteria led to the recommendation for multiple

lines was expressly an assumption. 15 ERCOT’s December 2024 sequencing letter stated that only

two of the three 765-kV import paths were needed by 2030. 16

         Applicants failed to show which two paths the sequencing letter referenced, whether the

system could meet the 2030 need without Import Path 2, or what reliability violation independently

requires Import Path 2 by 2030. Later models that include or assume all three paths do not supply

that missing analysis. The record therefore supports Finding of Fact Nos. 128–131.

E. Applicants’ Exception B.5: ERCOT’s Recommendation Does Not Override the
   Unsubstantiated Forecast

        Applicants except to Finding of Fact Nos. 132–140 and Conclusion of Law Nos. 13 and 14

and argue that 16 Texas Administrative Code § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II) requires the Commission

to give great weight to ERCOT’s PBRP recommendation. They also argue that the PFD lacked

countervailing expert evidence. The exception overlooks the lynchpin for the need argument; the

rule’s requirement that forecasted load growth be substantiated by quantifiable evidence. 17

        The record reflects that the load forecasts contained in the PBRP are simply not reliable.

Most projected non-oil-and-gas load was supported only by officer attestations or was

unconfirmed. In both cases, Applicants did not conduct any contract verification of these

projections from over the past several years. ERCOT later adopted a revised forecasting

methodology after actual experience showed that forecasted loads entered service below

originally-forecast levels. 18 Applicants did not retest the PBRP forecast under that methodology

or provide a project-specific analysis showing that Import Path 2 remained necessary after those

changes. Applicants’ own witnesses also confirmed that no study isolated Import Path 2 and did

not verify the forecast trajectory. 19

        Applicants therefore failed to show that the PBRP recommendation rests on the

quantifiable evidence required for great weight or that it outweighs the contrary evidence.

Continued inclusion of the paths in later planning models does not fill those gaps. The record

supports Finding of Fact Nos. 132–140, Conclusion of Law Nos. 13 and 14.




17
   16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II)
18

         Whitis respectfully requests that the Commission overrule Applicants’ Exception B.5 and

retain Finding of Fact Nos. 132–140 and Conclusion of Law Nos. 13 and 14.

F. Applicants’ Exception D.1 – D.4: Procedural Failures Cannot Be Remedied by An
   Extension.

        Applicants except to Finding of Fact Nos. 38–43 and Conclusion of Law Nos. 10, arguing

that they complied with the notice requirements of 16 TAC § 22.52 and that the Finding of Fact

Nos. 38-43 be removed and that Conclusion of Law No. 10 be replaced.

        The PFD properly rejected these arguments.

        16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3) requires that, on the date the application is filed, written notice be

mailed to all landowners “as stated on the current county tax rolls who would be directly affected

by the requested certificate.” 20

        Applicants pulled county tax records between December 8, 2025, and February 23, 2026,

but the Application was not filed until March 26, 2026. The appraisal districts continued updating

ownership information during that period. Applicants’ flawed process deprived more than three

dozen owners from timely notice, all of whom were directly affected by the proposed routes. 21

Applicants attempted to cure the lack of notice by sending supplemental notices to landowners.

However, some supplemental notices were not mailed until May 26 or June 1—approximately 67

days after filing, days before the hearing on the merits. 22

        Applicants failed to identify the full breadth of owners affected by the proposed routes.

This failure resulted in several landowners being deprived of any meaningful participation in the

contested case.




20
   16 Tex. Admin. Code § 22.52(a)(3).
21

22

Reply To Exceptions to Proposal for Decision                                                     Page 7 of 10
            Applicants point to the fact that owners were able to participate in the hearing. However,

Evidence that some owners overcame the delay does not establish compliance or negate the

practical loss of time.

           The rule provides a day-for-day extension of the proceedings as a remedy for insufficient

notice. But the 180-day statutory schedule does not allow for a worthwhile extension that rectifies

the lost time for affected parties.

           Because of this systemic failure and the inability to provide adequate time to parties, Whitis

respectfully requests the Commission overrule Applicants’ Exceptions D.1 – D.4 and retain

Finding of Fact Nos. 38-43 and Conclusion of Law No. 10.

                                 II.    REPLIES TO COMMISSION STAFF

A. Import Path 1 and ERCOT’s Recommendations Do Not Prove Import Path 2’s Need

           Commission Staff argues that ERCOT’s continuing recommendations and the

Commission’s Import Path 1 orders require a finding that Import Path 2 is needed. Staff also argues

that the PFD mischaracterized Mr. Poole’s testimony. The exception does not answer the PFD’s

two independent holdings: ERCOT’s recommendation did not qualify for great weight on this

record, and the greater weight of credible evidence rebutted it even if great weight applied. 23

As stated in Section 1.A. and 1.D., above, the need for Import Path 2 must stand on its own.

Approval of Import Path 1 therefore does not adjudicate the project-specific need for Import Path

2. 24

           Commission Staff’s exceptions argue that the testimony of its witness, Mr. Poole, was

mischaracterized. Staff’s argument suffers from the fatal assumption that Mr. Poole cannot state

that import paths are needed while, at the same time, question the accuracy of the Applicants’

supporting data. Despite the Staff-described expansive testimony on the need for Import Path 2,


23
     Staff’s Exceptions at 9–13; PFD at 90–92.
24
     Order Approving the Reliability Plan for the Permian Basin Region at 5 (Oct. 7, 2024).

Intervenor: Whitis Land Investments, LP
Reply To Exceptions to Proposal for Decision                                                  Page 8 of 10
 Mr. Poole unquestionably agreed that changed conditions may warrant reevaluation. 25 Further,

Mr. Poole confirmed that the studies did not show a current or projected service improvement for

Bell County ratepayers, even considering bidirectionality. 26 If anything, Mr. Poole’s expansive

testimony supporting import paths draws an irreconcilable and unavoidable contrast to his specific

concerns with the data for Import Path 2.

           Just as a Commission decision on Import Path 1 does not establish an independent need for

Import Path 2, it is possible for Mr. Poole to agree with the general need for import paths while

expressing concerns with the data used in the Import Path 2 applications. The ALJs properly

considered the entirety of Mr. Poole’s testimony in their ruling, without mischaracterization.

           Whitis respectfully requests that the Commission overrule Staff’s need exception and retain

the PFD’s findings and conclusions concerning Import Path 2.

                          III.     REPLIES TO ADDITIONAL EXCEPTIONS

           Whitis objects to further exceptions filed by additional parties. The exceptions align with

the exceptions filed by Applicants. For the sake of brevity, the exceptions are addressed below

with references to the replies above.

           A.      Staff exception regarding notice– see Section F above.

           B.      IV. Delaware Basin Midstream exceptions regarding need – see Sections A – E
                   above.

                                                IV.     PRAYER

           Whitis respectfully requests that the Commission overrule the foregoing Exceptions, adopt

the PFD’s findings and conclusions concerning notice and need, and deny the applications.

and argue that 16 Texas Administrative Code § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II) requires the Commission

to give great weight to ERCOT's PBRP recommendation. They also argue that the PFD lacked

countervailing expert evidence. The exception overlooks the lynchpin for the need argument; the

rule' s requirement that forecasted load growth be substantiated by quantifiable evidence. 17

        The record reflects that the load forecasts contained in the PBRP are simply not reliable.

Most projected non-oil-and-gas load was supported only by officer attestations or was

unconfirmed. In both cases, Applicants did not conduct any contract verification of these

projections from over the past several years. ERCOT later adopted a revised forecasting

methodology after actual experience showed that forecasted loads entered service below

originally-forecast levels.18 Applicants did not retest the PBRP forecast under that methodology

or provide a project-specific analysis showing that Import Path 2 remained necessary after those

changes. Applicants' own witnesses also confirmed that no study isolated Import Path 2 and did

not verify the forecast traj ectory. 19

        Applicants therefore failed to show that the PBRP recommendation rests on the

quantifiable evidence required for great weight or that it outweighs the contrary evidence.

Continued inclusion of the paths in later planning models does not fill those gaps. The record

supports Finding of Fact Nos. 132-140, Conclusion of Law Nos. 13 and 14.
